answer.answer:
To deliver a prefabricated timber facade whose panels never repeat, three things have to be in place at once: the panel geometry must come out of a design configurator riding on a standardised dimensional grid, so the variety sits in the data and not in the tooling; the fabricator has to be inside the design from the earliest phase, not handed a finished drawing; and the planning and logistics have to be precise, because moving the work into a factory moves the risk into scheduling. What you get back is better quality, fewer errors and less rework, a compressed programme and safer site work. What to watch is twofold: compliance for off-site work rests on third-party certification and traceability of the components, and a tightly integral architecture, where functions are bound to specific components, will fight exactly the interchangeability that non-repeating panels depend on; no named energy-performance standard, Minergie included, appears anywhere in this record, so nothing here speaks to that envelope target specifically.

**The dependency chain behind the facade**

Prefabrication/off-site (PR2) is activated in 20 of the 50 coded cases. Its own preconditions are explicit: PR2 depends on precise planning (RI14), because prefabrication relies on precise up-front planning and logistics [1] (peer-reviewed, DEP33), and RI14 is itself one of the most widely activated enablers in the set, at 36 of 50 cases. Alongside it, PR2 dependsOn RI18, because a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability [2] (peer-reviewed, DEP96). That is the closest the record comes to an envelope-certification question, and it is about component compliance and traceability, not thermal performance.

Three inbound paths feed PR2, all peer-reviewed: early involvement of the delivering production party, CO11 enablesCapability PR2, integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the manufacturer, fabricator or contractor to be involved in the early design phase, and a project delivery method that involves participants in early design should be selected [2] (DEP22); DfMA, PR9 enablesCapability PR2, orienting the project toward offsite manufacture [2] (DEP15); and supply chain integration, VA14 enablesCapability PR2 [2] (DEP79). CO11 is activated in 14 of 50 cases.

**Where the non-repeating panels come from**

The route to panel-by-panel variation runs through standardisation, not around it. AT7 enablesCapability AR6, on the standard ISO 2848, because modular coordination permits the interchangeability of different components [2] (DEP43), and AR6 enablesCapability PR11, because a design configurator integrates customisation data into robotic manufacturing [2] (peer-reviewed, DEP75). AR6 is activated in 12 of the 50 coded cases. The same standardisation node pays out twice more: AT7 enablesCapability VA7, the base module standard reducing component variety and coordinating design, manufacture and assembly [2] (DEP67, VA7 activated in 16 of 50), and AT7 enablesCapability VA21, standardisation of interfaces supporting interchangeability and system flexibility, a claim the source softens [2] (DEP90, VA21 activated in only 3 of 50, the weakest activation among the enablers retrieved here).

The counter-force is directional and explicit: AT1 constrains AT2, because integral architecture couples functions tightly to components, constraining modular interchange [2] (peer-reviewed, DEP59). AT1 is activated in 10 of 50 cases.

**What the off-site move returns**

All peer-reviewed outbound edges from PR2: PR2 enablesCapability VA2, offsite factory work compressing schedule [2] (DEP17); PR2 enablesCapability VA3, the controlled factory environment improving quality [2] (DEP18); PR2 enablesCapability VA10, factory-based offsite production improving quality control and reducing errors and rework [2] (DEP80); and PR2 enablesCapability VA13, moving work offsite improves site safety [3] (DEP19). VA13 is activated in 39 of 50 cases. PR2 carries 4 inbound and 6 outbound dependency edges in total, so this is the complete outbound picture for it.

If the ambition is a serial, industrialised line rather than one facade, note that AT8 dependsOn AT7, industrialised-construction scale depending on standardisation [2] (DEP31) and AT8 dependsOn RI12, adoption of digital fabrication at industrialised scale depending on adapted business models [2] (DEP81). AT8 is activated in 23 of 50 cases.

**Deployed record**

Timber facade work is present in the deployed cases. census_RXH10-2 performs assembly and timber joinery cutting, working on the structural core and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, adopted to address market, at technology readiness level 9 [4], and it uses timber [5]. Three off-site timber joinery processes sit at the same maturity: RP3 performs assembly and timber joinery cutting on the structural core, deployed off-site, at technology readiness level 9, adopted to address quality, integration and market [6]; RP6, same operations and placement, adopted to address digital, at technology readiness level 9 [7]; RP7, adopted to address digital and market, at technology readiness level 9 [8]. On the facade side, RP8 performs inspection and material handling on the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, deployed off-site, at technology readiness level 9, adopted to address digital, quality and labor [9], with RP17 doing facade inspection on site, outdoors, at technology readiness level 9 [10].
